h: Below decks on the emigrant ship
p: The moment most visitors remember at the Ulster American Folk Park is stepping aboard the emigrant ship. Between the Old World and the New World areas, you walk through a recreated dockside street and then on to a full-size replica sailing ship, ducking below deck to see the cramped bunks where families spent weeks crossing the Atlantic. It's dark, creaky and a little claustrophobic, and it brings home just how brave, or desperate, those travellers were.

It's worth making time for the smaller stories too. Many of the buildings are linked to real families, and the guides are full of tales about who lived where and what became of them in America. If you've got Ulster roots or relatives who emigrated, ask about the research facilities on site, as they can be a real help to anyone tracing family history.

Plan for a good few hours. The full outdoor trail is a proper walk, and with demonstrations to stop and watch, it's easy to lose track of time. Head round the Old World part first while everyone has energy, then cross over to the American side in the afternoon.

Omagh is a handy base for the west of Northern Ireland. Gortin Glen Forest Park, a short drive north, has forest drives and waymarked walks, and the Sperrin Mountains beyond offer big, quiet landscapes for a scenic run. The Strule and Camowen rivers meet in Omagh itself, and the town has shops and places to eat for when you're ready to refuel after your transatlantic adventure.
